Beacon's data model connects practice work to progress evidence. The record therefore preserves evidence behind progress and can show how demonstrated performance changes a skill rating. Skill assessment and readiness

Beacon describes skills diagnosis as an adaptive quiz that measures what a candidate can currently demonstrate. The SkillAssessment model documents the result as the candidate's proficiency for one skill compared with the level required by the target role. This distinction is important: proficiency is the candidate's current demonstrated level, while required_level is the benchmark for the role. The difference is used by the plan generator to create tasks. An assessment is therefore more than a quiz score displayed in isolation; it becomes structured evidence that can guide the next preparation activities and later progress review.

CandidateProfile exposes readiness_percent as a derived property rather than a separately stored value. It takes the assessments for that candidate, calculates proficiency divided by required level for each skill, caps each ratio at one, averages the ratios, and converts the result to a percentage. If there are no assessments, readiness is zero. Capping each skill at one prevents a very strong result in one area from hiding an unmet requirement in another area. If a required level is zero, that assessment contributes a ratio of one. The calculation measures progress against recorded skill requirements; it is not a prediction that an employer will make a particular hiring decision.

Skill blueprint and catalog

The README identifies the blueprint as a core product feature and notes that the role-to-skills mapping is cached per role across fields. It should be interpreted as a preparation guide, not a guarantee that every employer will ask the same questions. Different companies and interviewers can emphasize different skills, even for the same job title. The Skill model stores a competency as a shared catalog entry rather than leaving every assessment to invent its own skill wording. The catalog is important because candidates can then be compared against consistent skill labels and target-role requirements.
